title: The Twelve, the Strong Man, and Jesus' True Family
summary: Jesus heals a man's withered hand on the Sabbath, and the Pharisees begin plotting with the Herodians to kill him. Crowds pour in from every region, and Jesus appoints twelve apostles to be with him and to be sent out. His family thinks he is out of his mind, scribes from Jerusalem accuse him of driving out demons by Beelzebul, and Jesus answers with the parable of the strong man, a warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, and a declaration that whoever does God's will is his brother, sister, and mother.
story:
The chapter opens with the last of the five controversy stories that began at 2:1, and it closes that series with a plot to kill Jesus (verse 6), only a few pages into the Gospel. From here the lines are drawn. On one side, huge crowds come from Galilee, Judea, and the lands around, from as far south as Idumea and as far north as Tyre and Sidon, and Jesus forms a new community around himself, the Twelve. On the other, opposition hardens: scribes come down from Jerusalem to accuse him of working by the power of Satan, and even his own family sets out to take him home, convinced he has lost his mind.

The chapter asks the reader to decide what Jesus' power means. The unclean spirits say he is the Son of God; the scribes say he is possessed; his family says he is out of his mind. Jesus answers with his first parables, the strong man bound and his house plundered, and with a solemn warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. He then redefines his family: those seated around him doing the will of God. Chapter 4 will explain, through the parable of the sower, why the same word produces such different responses, and it will speak of ‘those outside’, the phrase this chapter uses of Jesus' own mother and brothers (verses 31 and 32).
historical:
The setting is still Galilee in the late 20s AD. The Herodians of verse 6 were supporters of Herod Antipas and the rule of the Herodian family. Pharisees, a religious renewal movement, and the partisans of a client king had little in common, and their alliance shows how widely Jesus was now seen as a threat. It was also ominous: Antipas had already arrested John the Baptist (1:14) and would execute him (6:14-29). The same pairing returns in Jerusalem, where Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus over taxes to Caesar (12:13).

The list of regions in verses 7 and 8 sketches the old land of Israel and its neighbors. Idumea, named only here in the New Testament, lay south of Judea and was the Edom of earlier times; the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus conquered it around 125 BC and required its people to be circumcised and to keep the Jewish law (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257-258), and Herod the Great's family came from there. ‘The region beyond the Jordan’ is Perea, east of the river, also ruled by Antipas. Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician cities on the coast to the northwest, largely Gentile, whose silver coinage was the standard currency for the temple tax. The crowd therefore includes people from every quarter of the old tribal territory and from beyond it, a fitting prelude to the choosing of twelve.

The names of the Twelve are known from four lists (here, Matthew 10:2-4, Luke 6:14-16, and Acts 1:13), which always begin with Peter and, where he appears, end with Judas. Thaddaeus here and in Matthew corresponds to ‘Judas son of James’ in Luke and Acts. Simon is called ho Kananaios, from an Aramaic word for zealous, which Luke translates as ‘the Zealot’. It may mean zeal for the law, or association with those who resisted Roman rule; the organized party called the Zealots is attested by Josephus only in the war of AD 66 to 70 (Jewish War 4.160-161). Iscariot is most often explained as Hebrew ish Qeriyyot, ‘man of Kerioth’, a town in southern Judah (Joshua 15:25), which would make Judas the one Judean among Galileans. Another suggestion links it to the Latin sicarius, ‘dagger man’, the name Josephus gives to assassins active in the 50s (Jewish War 2.254-257), but most scholars find that less likely. James and John were sons of Zebedee (1:19-20), and Andrew was Peter's brother (1:16).

That scribes ‘came down from Jerusalem’ (verse 22) signals that the religious authorities of the capital were now investigating Jesus. The brothers of Jesus are named in 6:3: James, Joses, Judas, and Simon. James later led the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19, Acts 15:13) and was executed there in AD 62, according to Josephus (Antiquities 20.200). Paul says the risen Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and Acts places Jesus' mother and brothers among the believers in Jerusalem after the ascension (Acts 1:14). The family that sets out to seize him in this chapter was later found inside the church.
cultural:
The Sabbath healing in verses 1 to 6 turned on a question every observant Jew recognized. The Mishnah states that any doubt about danger to life overrides the Sabbath (Yoma 8:6), and rabbinic law allowed treatment in emergencies. A withered hand was not an emergency; it could have waited until evening. Some groups were stricter still: the Damascus Document from Qumran forbids lifting an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath (CD 11:13-14). Jesus reframes the question. Doing nothing on the Sabbath was not neutral; to refuse to do good was to do harm, and while he asks whether it is lawful ‘to save life or to destroy it’ (verse 4), his questioners are already planning to destroy his.

Choosing twelve was a deliberate sign. Israel was made up of twelve tribes descended from the sons of Jacob, ten of them scattered since the Assyrian conquest, and prophets had promised that God would gather them again (Ezekiel 37:15-28). The Community Rule from Qumran describes the community's council as twelve men and three priests (1QS 8:1), probably for the same symbolic reason. By appointing twelve on a mountain, Jesus acts out the restoration of God's people around himself, and the scene may recall Moses on Sinai, where twelve pillars stood for the twelve tribes (Exodus 24:4). Renaming carried weight too. In Scripture a new name often marks a new calling given by God (Abram to Abraham in Genesis 17:5, Jacob to Israel in Genesis 32:28). Simon becomes Peter, from petros, rock (Aramaic kēpha), and James and John become Boanerges, which Mark translates ‘Sons of Thunder’, though the Aramaic behind the Greek form is uncertain.

Family was the center of honor, identity, livelihood, and care in the ancient Mediterranean world. A son who left his trade to wander as a preacher, drawing crowds so large he could not eat and conflict with the authorities from Jerusalem, brought shame on his relatives and could bring danger. That is the background to their attempt to ‘take custody of Him’ (verse 21); the verb, kratēsai, is the one Mark later uses for his arrest (14:1, 14:46). A teacher's disciples sat around him to learn; the Mishnah preserves the counsel that one should sit in the dust at the feet of the sages (Avot 1:4). When Jesus looks at the circle seated around him and names them his mother and brothers, he places the community of learners above the family of blood, a claim that would have sounded radical and even dishonorable.

The charge that Jesus drove out demons by Beelzebul was an accusation of sorcery, a capital offense in the law (Exodus 22:18, Deuteronomy 18:10-12). The name probably comes from Baal-zebul, ‘Prince Baal’, a title known from texts at Ugarit, which Israel mocked as Baal-zebub, ‘lord of flies’, the god of the Philistine city of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2). By Jesus' time it had become a name for the chief of demons. The accusation outlived him. Justin Martyr, writing around 160, reports that Jewish opponents called Jesus a magician and a deceiver of the people (Dialogue with Trypho 69); the pagan critic Celsus claimed he had learned magical powers in Egypt (Origen, Against Celsus 1.28); and the Babylonian Talmud preserves a tradition that Jesus was executed for practicing sorcery and leading Israel astray (Sanhedrin 43a). No one in these sources denied that Jesus did remarkable things; the dispute was over the power behind them.
literary:
The chapter falls into three movements. Verses 1 to 6 close the chain of controversies that began at 2:1, returning to the synagogue and the Sabbath where the Galilean ministry began (1:21) and ending in a plot. Verses 7 to 19 turn outward and upward: a summary of Jesus' work by the sea, with crowds from every region and spirits falling before him, followed by the appointment of the Twelve on the mountain. This pattern, a summary followed by a scene with the disciples, opens a new section of the Gospel just as 1:14-20 did and 6:6-13 will.

Verses 20 to 35 are one of Mark's characteristic sandwiches, which James R. Edwards studied in Novum Testamentum (1989). The story of Jesus' family setting out to seize him (verses 20 and 21) is interrupted by the scribes' accusation and Jesus' reply (22 to 30), and then resumed when his mother and brothers arrive (31 to 35). The two stories interpret each other. Family and scribes both misjudge Jesus, the one saying he is out of his mind, the other that he is possessed, and both are set against the circle sitting around him. The movement from inside to outside is marked by the words themselves: at the start his family comes to seize him, and at the end his mother and brothers stand ‘outside’ (exō, verses 31 and 32) while a crowd sits ‘around Him’ (verses 32 and 34).

Jesus answers the scribes ‘in parables’ (verse 23), the first time Mark uses the word, preparing for chapter 4. His reply is built with care: a question (how can Satan drive out Satan?), three parallel conditions about a divided kingdom, a divided house, and a divided Satan, each ending ‘cannot stand’, and then the image that turns the argument: the strong man bound and his house plundered. Verse 28 begins ‘Truly I tell you’ (amēn legō hymin), the first of about a dozen such solemn sayings in Mark, and verse 30 adds the narrator's explanation so the reader cannot miss what provoked the warning. Two details look ahead to the passion: Judas is introduced as the one ‘who betrayed Jesus’ (verse 19), and the verb for seizing him (21) will be the verb of the arrest.

outline.t: A withered hand healed on the Sabbath; the plot begins
Crowds from every region and spirits silenced
Jesus' family thinks he is out of his mind
The Beelzebul accusation and the strong man

doctrines.note: Jesus appoints the Twelve ‘to accompany Him, to be sent out to preach’ (verse 14), the two movements of the church's life: being with Christ and being sent by him. He then redefines his family as all who do God's will, a community bound not by blood but by obedience, with himself at its center.

The parable of the strong man interprets Jesus' exorcisms as the invasion of Satan's house by one stronger. The divided kingdom that cannot stand (verse 24) is set against the kingdom of God, which arrives as the liberation of those held captive by evil.

The scribes look at the Spirit's work in Jesus, the same Spirit who descended on him at the Jordan (1:10), and call it the work of an unclean spirit (verse 30). Jesus warns that such blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven. The chapter treats the Spirit as the power by which Jesus binds the strong man, and rejecting that power as rejecting the only source of forgiveness.

Jesus promises that the sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies, with one warning: those who call the Spirit's work evil place themselves outside forgiveness. The chapter also shows sin as hardness of heart (verse 5), a refusal to see good done because it breaks one's own rules.

Jesus asks whether it is lawful on the Sabbath “to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it” (verse 4). He treats the day of rest as a day for restoring life, and he heals by a word alone, without any act that could be called work.

words.note: Apostolos, apostle, one who is sent, a messenger with authority to represent the sender. It occurs about eighty times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke-Acts and Paul, and twice in Mark (here in verse 14, where some manuscripts lack it, and 6:30). The related verb apostellō, to send, stands in the same verse. The later church extended the title to others commissioned by the risen Christ, such as Paul, but in the Gospels it belongs chiefly to the Twelve.

Pōrōsis, hardening, hardness. It occurs only three times in the New Testament: here, in Romans 11:25 of Israel's partial hardening, and in Ephesians 4:18 of Gentile hearts. The related verb pōroō describes the disciples' own hearts in Mark (6:52, 8:17). The word pictures a callus, insensitivity that has grown over time. Jesus is grieved by a hardness that would rather see a man stay crippled than see a rule bent.

Orgē, anger, wrath. It occurs thirty-six times in the New Testament, most often of God's judgment, and only here in Mark. Mark alone reports that Jesus looked around ‘with anger and sorrow’ (verse 5); Matthew omits the emotion and Luke keeps only the look. The anger is directed at hardness of heart and joined to grief, the only place in the Gospels where the word describes Jesus.

Ischyros, strong, mighty. It occurs twenty-nine times in the New Testament and three times in Mark: John the Baptist announced one ‘more powerful’ than himself (1:7), and here the strong man is Satan, whose house can be plundered only by one who first binds him (verse 27). The implication is that Jesus is the stronger one John promised. The image has roots in Isaiah 49:24-25, where the LORD promises that “the captives of the mighty will be taken away.”

Beelzeboul, Beelzebul. It occurs seven times in the New Testament, all in the first three Gospels (Matthew 10:25, 12:24, 12:27; Mark 3:22; Luke 11:15, 18, 19). It probably preserves the Canaanite title Baal-zebul, ‘Prince Baal’, which Israel parodied as Baal-zebub, ‘lord of flies’ (2 Kings 1:2). The scribes use it as a name for the prince of demons, and Jesus treats it as another name for Satan (verse 23).

Blasphēmia, blasphemy, slander, speech that insults God or injures another. It occurs eighteen times in the New Testament and three times in Mark (3:28, 7:22, 14:64); the related verb appears in verses 28 and 29. The scribes had charged Jesus with blasphemy for forgiving sins (2:7); now Jesus warns that attributing the Spirit's work to Satan is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. At his trial the charge will be turned against him again (14:64).

Thelēma, will, desire. It occurs sixty-two times in the New Testament and only here in Mark. BDAG treats it both as what one wishes and as what one purposes or commands. Doing ‘the will of God’ (verse 35) defines Jesus' family, and Mark will show Jesus himself praying in Gethsemane ‘not what I will, but what You will’ (14:36, using the verb thelō), so that the family of Jesus is defined by the same obedience he practiced.

Parabolē, parable, comparison. It occurs fifty times in the New Testament, nearly all in the first three Gospels, and thirteen times in Mark, first here in verse 23. In the Greek Old Testament it translates Hebrew mashal, a word covering proverbs, riddles, taunts, and extended comparisons. Jesus' first parables in Mark are short images of a divided kingdom, a divided house, and a bound strong man, answering hostile questioners with pictures that require them to think.

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as the stronger one who has come to bind the strong man and free his captives. Isaiah had asked, “Can the plunder be snatched from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be delivered?” and answered with the LORD's promise, “Even the captives of the mighty will be taken away” (Isaiah 49:24-25). Jesus claims that this rescue is happening in his exorcisms: Satan is not divided, he is being defeated. Christian readers have long heard in this an echo of the first promise that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15), though the link is thematic, not a quotation. John had announced one ‘more powerful’ than himself (1:7), and the same word, strong, returns here. Mark will show that the binding of Satan is completed not by exorcism alone but by the Son of Man's death and resurrection.

Jesus also acts as Israel's God acts. He goes up on the mountain, calls ‘those He wanted’, and appoints twelve, as God formed a people of twelve tribes; he gives new names, as God renamed Abram and Jacob. The unclean spirits fall before him and cry, “You are the Son of God” (verse 11), and he silences them, because that confession will be made rightly only at the cross (15:39). The Spirit who came upon him at the Jordan is at work in his exorcisms, so that to call his work unclean is to blaspheme the Spirit.

Yet the chapter shows his humanity as sharply as any in the Gospels. He looks around ‘with anger and sorrow’ at hard hearts (verse 5). He is pressed by crowds until he cannot eat (verse 20). He is misunderstood by his own family, who think he has lost his mind, a grief that the Psalms and the prophets knew (Psalm 69:8, Jeremiah 12:6). And the plot to kill him in verse 6 shows that his road to the cross is set early. The chapter ends with Jesus at the center of a new family, looking at those around him and calling them mother and brothers and sisters: the Son gathers children for the Father, and the will of God is the bond that makes them one.
interpretation:
The chapter's sayings drew early and lasting comment. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.8.2, around 180) read the strong man as the devil, strong only in comparison with us, and Christ as the one who bound him and set the weak free. Augustine (City of God 20.7) used the same saying to interpret the binding of Satan in Revelation 20, holding that Satan was bound at Christ's first coming so that he cannot prevent the nations from believing, a reading that became the basis of the amillennial view held by much of the Western church. Tertullian (On the Flesh of Christ 7) answered Marcion and Apelles, who used ‘Who are My mother and My brothers?’ to deny that Christ was truly born, by arguing that one who rebukes his relatives does not deny that he has them.

The warning about blasphemy against the Spirit has one of the longest and most painful histories of any saying in the Gospels. The Didache (11:7) applied it to testing traveling prophets: one must not test or judge a prophet speaking in the Spirit, for every sin will be forgiven but not that one. Augustine devoted a sermon to it (Sermon 71) and concluded that the sin is final impenitence, a hardness that refuses forgiveness until death. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 14) gathered the patristic readings. Calvin (Institutes 3.3.22) defined it as deliberate, malicious resistance to truth one knows to be God's. John Bunyan, in Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners (1666), described years of terror that he had committed it and his slow discovery that he had not, and Bertrand Russell, in his lecture Why I Am Not a Christian (1927), cited the saying as a cause of great misery to sensitive people and a mark against Jesus' character.

The family scene became the center of a long debate about the brothers of Jesus. The second-century Protevangelium of James presented them as Joseph's sons by an earlier marriage, the view Epiphanius of Salamis defended (Panarion 78) and the Eastern churches hold. Helvidius, in Rome, argued that they were sons of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus; Jerome answered him in Against Helvidius (383), arguing that they were cousins, the view that became standard in the Latin West. Luther and Zwingli retained Mary's perpetual virginity; many later Protestants adopted Helvidius's reading. Modern scholarship took up Mark's portrait of Jesus' family: the ecumenical team of Protestant and Catholic scholars behind Mary in the New Testament (1978, edited by Raymond Brown, Karl Donfried, Joseph Fitzmyer, and John Reumann) concluded that Mark's picture of the family, Mary included, is a negative one.

The chapter also shaped modern readings of the whole Gospel. Ched Myers took the strong man for the title of his political commentary, Binding the Strong Man (1988), reading Jesus' ministry as a challenge to the powers that held Galilee captive, and James R. Edwards's study of Markan sandwiches (1989) made verses 20 to 35 a standard example of the technique. Jewish readers have noted how early the charge of sorcery appears in Jewish and pagan sources, and have read the scribes' accusation as an attempt to explain real healings within their own categories. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year B, 2:23-3:6 is read on Proper 4 and 3:20-35 on Proper 5, in early June.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter. In verse 14 the clause “whom He designated as apostles” is in Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus but missing from many other manuscripts; some editors suspect it came in from Luke 6:13, and some versions print it in brackets or a note. Verse 16 in some manuscripts repeats ‘He appointed the twelve’ before the list, a clause the BSB renders “These are the twelve He appointed”; the King James Version, following the later text, begins the list more simply.

In verse 18 the Greek Kananaios was rendered ‘the Canaanite’ in the King James Version, as if it named a place, but it comes from the Aramaic word for zealous, and modern versions render ‘the Zealot’ or ‘the Cananaean’. Some manuscripts read Lebbaeus for Thaddaeus. In verse 21 the phrase hoi par autou, literally ‘those from beside him’, can mean his friends or associates (so the KJV) or his family, and most modern versions read family, since his mother and brothers arrive in verse 31. Some manuscripts, including Codex Bezae, soften the verse so that the scribes and others, not his family, set out to seize him.

In verse 22 the form Beelzebub in the King James Version comes from the Latin Vulgate and the Syriac, which assimilated the name to Baal-zebub of 2 Kings 1:2; the Greek manuscripts read Beelzeboul or, in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, Beezeboul. In verse 29 modern editions read ‘an eternal sin’ (hamartēmatos), while the later manuscripts behind the King James Version read ‘eternal judgment’ (kriseōs), which the KJV renders ‘eternal damnation’; the harder word, sin, is better attested. In verse 32 some manuscripts, including Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Bezae, add ‘and your sisters’; the 27th edition of Nestle-Aland printed the words, and the 28th edition and the SBL Greek New Testament leave them out.

teach.big: Jesus is the stronger one who binds Satan and gathers a new family around himself, and every person must decide whether his power comes from God, since to call the Spirit's liberating work evil is to refuse the only source of forgiveness.

outline.t: Doing nothing is not neutral: Jesus restores a man on the Sabbath, grieves over hard hearts, and the rule-keepers answer by plotting to destroy life.
People come from every direction for what Jesus can do, but he refuses the demons' testimony; knowing the right words about Jesus is not the same as following him.
Jesus calls whom he wants, first to be with him and then to be sent, and he forms a renewed Israel out of ordinary and even opposite people, including one who would betray him.
The people closest to Jesus can misjudge him most; his own family thinks devotion to his mission is madness.
Jesus' exorcisms are not Satan fighting himself but the invasion of Satan's house by one stronger, who binds him and sets his captives free.
The breadth of God's forgiveness is vast, and the one danger is to call the Spirit's work of liberation evil and so refuse the only source of pardon.
Jesus' true family is gathered around him and defined by doing God's will, a family open to anyone, including those whose own families have failed them.

teach.pitfalls:
The chief danger in teaching this chapter is the unforgivable sin. Presented carelessly, verses 28 and 29 have terrified tender consciences for centuries. The text itself frames the warning: it is addressed to scribes who had seen Jesus free people from evil and called it the work of the devil (verse 30), and it follows the broadest promise of forgiveness in the Gospel (verse 28). Teachers should say plainly that anxious fear of having committed this sin is itself evidence of a heart that has not hardened against God.

A second pitfall is to read verses 31 to 35 as Jesus rejecting his mother and family or as a charter for abandoning one's relatives. Jesus does not deny them; he names a deeper bond, and his family later appears among the believers (Acts 1:14). A third is to use verse 21 to settle the debate about Mary's virginity or the identity of Jesus' brothers, questions on which faithful Christians differ and which the verse does not address. A fourth is to treat the Pharisees of verses 1 to 6 as types of all Jews; Mark is describing particular opponents, and Jesus and the Twelve are Jews. Finally, avoid making the Twelve into a list of personality types; Mark gives almost no detail about most of them, and his point is that Jesus chose them, not that they were remarkable.
teach.pastoral: Three groups in any congregation will feel this chapter. The first are people who fear they have committed the unforgivable sin, often those who struggle with scrupulosity or obsessive doubt; they need to hear that the warning is addressed to hardened opponents and that the desire for God is itself a sign of the Spirit's work. Teach verse 28 as warmly as verse 29 is serious, and encourage anyone tormented by this fear to talk with a pastor or a counselor. The second are people estranged from their families or misunderstood by them, including those whose faith has cost them relationships; Jesus knew this grief and offers a family defined by God's will. The third are people who have been called crazy, or who live with mental illness; be careful never to use ‘out of his mind’ (verse 21) as a joke, and remember that Jesus himself bore the label.

hard.q: What is the unforgivable sin, and could someone commit it without knowing?
hard.a:
The objection is moral as well as exegetical. If God's mercy is infinite, how can any sin be beyond forgiveness, and why would Jesus speak words that have caused so much fear? Bertrand Russell, in his 1927 lecture Why I Am Not a Christian, singled out this saying as having caused untold misery to people who imagined they had committed the sin, and judged that a teacher of real kindliness would not have put such terror into the world. John Bunyan's autobiography, Grace Abounding (1666), bears out Russell's observation from the inside: for years Bunyan believed he had committed the sin and was beyond hope.

Christian interpreters have answered from the context and from the logic of forgiveness. Mark explains the saying: ‘He has an unclean spirit’ (verse 30). The scribes had seen the Spirit's plain work of liberation and called it Satan's; the sin is not a careless word or a doubt, but a settled refusal to recognize God's work when it is seen, and so a refusal of the one through whom forgiveness comes. Augustine (Sermon 71) identified it with final impenitence, the hardness that refuses forgiveness to the end; Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 14) gathered this and other readings; and Calvin (Institutes 3.3.22) described it as deliberate resistance to known truth for the sake of resisting. On all these readings it is unforgivable not because God's mercy runs out, but because the person has shut the door through which mercy comes. Pastors from Bunyan's day to ours have noted that those who fear they have committed it show, by their very fear and longing for God, that they have not. The same passage opens with the widest promise of forgiveness in the Gospel, that all sins and blasphemies will be forgiven. Interpreters differ on whether the sin can be committed today in the same form, since it was spoken of those who saw Jesus' works in person, but they agree that it is not a trap for the anxious.

hard.q: Did Jesus' own family think he was insane, and how does that fit with the Gospels' birth stories and the church's teaching about Mary?
hard.a:
The objection is that Mark, the earliest Gospel, has no birth narrative and presents Jesus' family as unbelieving: they come to seize him, saying ‘He is out of His mind’ (verse 21), and when they arrive he points past them to those who do God's will. John 7:5 adds, “For even His own brothers did not believe in Him.” Critical scholars conclude that Mark shows no knowledge of an annunciation or a virginal conception, and that Luke's picture of a Mary who treasured the angel's words is hard to square with a mother who thought her son had lost his mind. The ecumenical team of Protestant and Catholic scholars behind Mary in the New Testament (1978) concluded that Mark's picture of the family, including Mary, is negative. A second debate concerns the brothers. Helvidius in the fourth century, and many Protestants since, have read them as sons of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus, the plainest sense of the word.

Responses differ. Some note that verse 21 does not name Mary, that ‘those from beside him’ may mean relatives or friends more broadly, and that a family could act from fear for his safety after the plot of verse 6 as well as from embarrassment; others grant that Mark portrays the family as uncomprehending and read that as part of his theme that even those closest to Jesus fail to understand him until after Easter. Luke himself says Mary did not understand at times (Luke 2:50) and kept things in her heart (2:19, 2:51), and Acts places Mary and the brothers among the believers (Acts 1:14), with James becoming a leader after the risen Jesus appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7). On the brothers, the Eastern churches, following the Protevangelium of James and Epiphanius, hold that they were Joseph's sons by an earlier marriage; the Roman Catholic Church, following Jerome's Against Helvidius (383), holds that they were cousins or close relatives; and many Protestants hold that they were Mary's younger sons, while Luther and other Reformers kept the older view. The chapter does not settle that question, and Christians who differ on it can agree on what the chapter says: that belonging to Jesus is finally a matter of doing God's will.

observe: List everyone in this chapter who says who or what Jesus is. What does each say?
What does Mark say the Twelve were appointed for in verses 14 and 15?
Where are Jesus' mother and brothers in verses 31 to 35, and where is the crowd?
interpret: Why were the Pharisees willing to join the Herodians against Jesus after a healing on the Sabbath?
How does the parable of the strong man answer the charge that Jesus works by Satan's power?
What exactly had the scribes done that led Jesus to warn about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (verse 30)?
apply: Jesus called the Twelve first to be with him and then to be sent. Which of those two callings is weaker in your life right now?
Where have you seen good done and been tempted to find a reason to disapprove because it broke your expectations?
Jesus says whoever does God's will is his brother, sister, and mother. How should that shape the way your church treats people who have no family or have been cut off by theirs?
